description: Manually curated STRIDE ground truth for the Web Application with Authentication architecture. Each threat is keyed by its target (component_id or data_flow_id) plus STRIDE category; that (target, category) pair is the intended matching key for evaluation. This architecture introduces trust-boundary crossings and a third-party payment provider, so several threats arise from relationships between components rather than from a single attribute. Well-secured flows (encrypted + authenticated, e.g. api_to_db, api_to_auth, api_to_payment) intentionally carry no ground-truth threats so they can surface false positives.

threats.description: The internet-exposed frontend can be impersonated by phishing or lookalike sites tricking users into submitting credentials.
threats.mitigation: Serve over HSTS-enforced TLS, use verified domains, and educate users; pin the auth origin.

threats.description: Client-side code and requests from the internet-exposed frontend can be manipulated (e.g. tampered payloads, DOM/script injection).
threats.mitigation: Apply Content Security Policy, integrity checks (SRI), and server-side validation of all inputs.

threats.description: As a public entry point, the frontend can be overwhelmed by volumetric or application-layer traffic.
threats.mitigation: Use a CDN/WAF, rate limiting, and autoscaling for static delivery.

threats.description: The internet-exposed backend API can be targeted by clients impersonating legitimate users or replaying tokens.
threats.mitigation: Validate access tokens on every request, enforce short token lifetimes, and check audience/issuer.

threats.description: The API can receive manipulated or malicious requests (parameter tampering, injection payloads).
threats.mitigation: Validate and sanitize all inputs, use parameterized queries, and enforce strict schema validation.

threats.description: Without sufficient audit logging, clients can deny performing sensitive actions such as payments.
threats.mitigation: Log authenticated requests with tamper-evident, timestamped audit trails.

threats.description: As a public internet-facing endpoint, the API is exposed to denial-of-service attacks.
threats.mitigation: Apply rate limiting, request throttling, timeouts, and upstream DDoS protection.

threats.description: Flaws in authorization logic could let an authenticated client access resources beyond its privileges.
threats.mitigation: Enforce least-privilege authorization on every endpoint and separate roles/scopes.

threats.description: The internet-exposed authentication service is a prime target for credential stuffing and brute-force impersonation.
threats.mitigation: Enforce MFA, account lockout/backoff, and anomaly detection on login attempts.

threats.description: The auth service stores sensitive credential material (password hashes, tokens, keys) that could be exposed.
threats.mitigation: Store only salted hashes, encrypt secrets at rest, and tightly restrict access.

threats.description: Weaknesses in token issuance or role assignment could allow privilege escalation across the whole system.
threats.mitigation: Validate token claims and scopes, sign tokens with rotated keys, and audit role grants.

threats.description: Overwhelming the public auth service can lock out all users by preventing logins.
threats.mitigation: Rate-limit login endpoints and isolate auth capacity from general API traffic.

threats.description: The application database stores sensitive data exposable via misconfiguration, backups, or compromised credentials.
threats.mitigation: Encrypt data at rest, restrict network/account access, and manage secrets securely.

threats.description: Sensitive records could be modified without authorization if database access controls are weak.
threats.mitigation: Enforce least-privilege database accounts and integrity constraints; monitor write access.

threats.description: Without database audit logging, changes to sensitive data cannot be reliably attributed.
threats.mitigation: Enable database audit logging for access to and modification of sensitive tables.

threats.description: The initial browser-to-frontend flow is unauthenticated, allowing session fixation or man-in-the-middle impersonation attempts before login.
threats.mitigation: Establish authenticated sessions promptly, use secure cookies, and enforce HSTS.

threats.description: The credential-submission flow from frontend to auth is unauthenticated at initiation and susceptible to interception or CSRF-style abuse.
threats.mitigation: Use anti-CSRF tokens, PKCE for OAuth flows, and bind the flow to a verified origin.

threats.description: This flow carries raw credentials; weaknesses in transport or logging could expose secrets.
threats.mitigation: Enforce TLS, never log credentials, and use short-lived authorization codes instead of raw secrets.

threats.description: Payment data crosses a trust boundary to a third-party provider; misrouting or logging could disclose cardholder data.
threats.mitigation: Minimize transmitted data (tokenization), pin the provider certificate, and avoid logging payloads.
